corridor.boundaryRule: Create the next eastward Shaelvien-owned zone when documented material or structural change is substantial enough that the current gameplay model no longer accurately represents the next historical arc.

contentProfile.principle: Mature-rated presentation is allowed in Shaelvien. Content rating does not change historical provenance: FACT still requires cited evidence, RECONSTRUCTION remains bounded interpretation, and FICTION remains connective narrative.
contentProfile.historicalIntegrityRule: Do not invent, suppress, or relabel historical claims merely to force a particular content rating.

provenanceLegend.FACT: Directly supported by the cited archaeological record.
provenanceLegend.RECONSTRUCTION: A bounded playable interpretation required to turn evidence into an action; not itself a discovered fact.
provenanceLegend.FICTION: Narrative connective tissue only. It may not contradict or masquerade as evidence.

history.text: Lomekwi 3 is a 3.3-million-year-old archaeological site in West Turkana, Kenya, with in situ stone artefacts in a wooded palaeoenvironment.
The assemblage shows battering activities and core reduction, indicating developing knowledge of stone fracture properties.
The taxonomic identity of the toolmakers is not established by the site. The campaign must not assign them to Homo or another species as a fact.

lore.text: The player's journey supplies unnamed companions, immediate choices, and continuity between evidence points. These relationships are fictional and may never be presented as archaeological discovery.

history.text: Stone artefacts were recovered in situ and from the surface at LOM3.
The published assemblage includes unusually large cores, relatively few flaking surfaces, and extensive battering/percussive evidence.

lore.text: Gameplay places the player beside a working stone surface so the documented actions can be performed. The exact sequence, participants, motives, and social setting are not preserved.

instance.name: LOM3 Tool-Making Locality
instance.objective: Reproduce only the documented classes of stone-working action, then preserve the uncertainty.
facts: 3.3 Ma age for the archaeological site.

tasks.label: Read the stone
tasks.historicalBasis: The published interpretation describes developing understanding of stone fracture properties.
tasks.action: Compare candidate stone surfaces and predict which impact is most likely to fracture.

tasks.label: Stabilize the core
tasks.historicalBasis: The assemblage includes large cores and percussive/battering activities.
tasks.action: Choose a stable support/orientation for a large core before impact.

tasks.label: Batter
tasks.historicalBasis: Battering activities are directly reported for LOM3.
tasks.action: Perform controlled repeated percussion and observe the resulting damage.

tasks.label: Reduce the core
tasks.historicalBasis: Core reduction is directly reported for LOM3.
tasks.action: Attempt to detach material from the core without introducing later stone-tool techniques.

tasks.label: Record the result
tasks.historicalBasis: Modern recording is a game mechanic used to teach the evidence and uncertainty.
tasks.action: Compare the result to the factual evidence summary; do not promote the player's successful method into historical fact.

languageContext.original: No written or recorded language survives.

fictionalDialogue.label: Gameplay rendering
fictionalDialogue.text: Characters may communicate through game dialogue or gesture for continuity, but no words, grammar, names, or language family may be presented as historical.

bridge.rule: After the factual tasks resolve, fictional continuity may move the party forward in time only toward a separately verified archaeological node.

playableReconstruction.rule: Player actions reconstruct documented classes of stone-working behavior. A successful reconstruction is never promoted into a historical claim.

forbiddenWithoutEvidence: controlled fire as a Lomekwi 3 fact

sources.citation: Harmand, S. et al. 3.3-million-year-old stone tools from Lomekwi 3, West Turkana, Kenya. Nature 521, 310–315 (2015).
